problems.description: ClientRegistry is guarded by a threading.Lock but accessed from the asyncio loop and (per its own docstring) worker threads — mixing threading and async concurrency models invites subtle ordering bugs; the registry is only ever touched from async code here, so an asyncio.Lock or loop-single-threaded access would be simpler.

14 convention violations measured by static analysis (score 0.71): test files (conftest.py, test_channels.py, test_expiry.py, test_history.py) use non-PascalCase class names and non-UPPERCASE module-level constants.
Bare `except Exception` in _send_to/_send_to_all silently swallows all send failures and drops clients with no logging — hard to diagnose disconnect storms or serialization errors.
Full stack swap: discards the existing Flask/sqlite seam for two new async dependencies (websockets, aiohttp) in one session; justified by greenfield scope but leaves the seed stack unused.
Test suite added (+3 test files + conftest) with convention violations present, suggesting fixtures/classes were written hastily rather than per project style.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: ClientRegistry (connection state) vs NotificationServer (protocol/behavior) vs message encoding helpers.
Message model is explicit and validated: VALID_TYPES whitelist, uniform {type, payload, timestamp} envelope with UTC ISO timestamps.
Thread-safety is consciously designed and documented rather than incidental.
Graceful lifecycle handling: dead clients are removed from the registry during send and on disconnect.
Consistent type hints and docstrings on all public methods.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield implementation of the notification-service target architecture (registry + async server + typed broadcast/direct/system messages + health check) that improves on the placeholder todo seed, but it discards the existing stack and style wholesale and carries the measured 0.71 convention score (test-file class/constant naming) plus a threading/asyncio mix and broad exception swallowing as debt.

problems.description: The channel-extraction expression `message.get("channel") or payload.get("channel")` is duplicated verbatim three times in _dispatch (broadcast, subscribe, unsubscribe); a small `_extract_channel` helper would remove the repetition.

Mechanical measurements report 14 convention violations (convention score 0.71) — Classes should use PascalCase and module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE in the generated test files (conftest.py, test_channels.py, test_expiry.py, test_history.py). These are confined to test scaffolding, not the new app.py logic.

_send_to_channel awaits each websocket.send sequentially rather than batching with asyncio.gather; this matches the existing _send_to_all pattern, so it is consistent, but could be a throughput bottleneck on large channels.
subscribe/unsubscribe produce no ack to the sender (unlike the 'system' branch which acks), so clients have no confirmation their subscription succeeded.

strengths: ChannelRegistry mirrors the existing ClientRegistry lock-guarded, thread-safe pattern, so the new subsystem slots cleanly into the established architecture.
The broadcast signature extension (`channel: str | None = None`) is fully backwards compatible — existing broadcast callers are unaffected.
Disconnect cleanup is correct: handler's finally block calls channels.unsubscribe_all(client_id), preventing stale channel memberships.
New REST endpoints follow the exact handler style of _health_handler (aiohttp json_response) and are registered in the same router block.
Module docstring and VALID_TYPES were updated in sync with the new message types, keeping documentation and validation consistent.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted, pattern-respecting feature addition that generalizes the existing registry design to channels with proper thread-safety and cleanup; the only convention shortfall is confined to generated test files.

problems.description: 14 convention violations across conftest.py, test_channels.py, test_expiry.py, test_history.py (classes not PascalCase, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE); mechanical convention score 0.71. Notably the violations are concentrated in test files — the runtime code in app.py follows project conventions.
fakeredis.aioredis is imported unconditionally while the redis package itself is optional-guarded; production runtime now hard-depends on a test-oriented fake broker library.
_listen_loop swallows all non-cancellation exceptions silently with a bare 0.05s retry sleep — deserialization or broker failures would be invisible with no logging.
stop() chains getattr('aclose'/'close') fallbacks under BaseException; defensive but adds surface area where redis-asyncio vs fakeredis API drift could hide cleanup failures.

strengths: Redis pub/sub envelope backbone with routing metadata (all/channel/direct/system) and documented double-delivery avoidance — publishing instance relies on its own subscription rather than a local copy.
fakeredis fallback keeps the server runnable and testable without a broker, with REDIS_URL opt-in for production.
Client connection state (incl. channel subscriptions) mirrored into Redis for restart survival — a coherent durability story.
Clean class separation (RedisBroker, MessageStore) with typed signatures, docstrings, and consistent style matching the existing ChannelRegistry pattern.
SQLite message history (DATABASE_URL with in-memory default) exposed via GET /messages.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-designed integration commit adding a Redis pub/sub multi-instance backbone and SQLite persistence with a documented envelope/durability design, held back by systematic test-file naming violations (0.71 convention score) and minor robustness/dependency smells (silent exception swallowing, unconditional fakeredis import).

problems.description: WebSocketTransport crosses the abstraction boundary by calling private server members (server._dispatch, server.send_system) rather than going through a defined interface on BaseTransport.

The abstract send_message/broadcast contract encodes WebSocket-specific failure semantics (dropping unreachable clients) in the base interface, so alternate transports inherit behavior that may not suit them.

Mechanical convention score of 0.71 is driven by 14 violations in conftest.py and test files (lower-case classes, non-UPPER constants) that are NOT part of this diff; the commit's own additions (PascalCase BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport, DEFAULT_TRANSPORT constant) are compliant.
Broad except Exception: pass in on_connect swallows address-extraction errors silently, masking the actual failure mode.

strengths: Clean pluggable-transport abstraction (BaseTransport ABC) with a coherent lifecycle contract: start/stop/on_connect/on_disconnect/send_message/broadcast
Backwards compatible: WebSocketTransport remains the default and TRANSPORT env var is opt-in, so existing deployments are unaffected
Factory function get_transport resolves name/alias ('websocket'/'ws') with explicit unknown-transport error handling
Reuses existing ClientRegistry/ChannelRegistry/RedisBroker via properties rather than duplicating infrastructure
Docstrings and type hints match the existing module style (including UPPER_CASE default constant convention)
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, backwards-compatible transport-abstraction refactor that cleanly isolates WebSocket mechanics from core notification logic — the low mechanical convention score reflects pre-existing violations in test files outside this commit while the commit's own code adheres to conventions.

problems.description: 14 convention violations reported, all confined to new test files (conftest.py, test_channels.py, test_expiry.py, test_history.py): test classes named in PascalCase rather than snake_case and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE.

New RedisBroker.redis property exposes the internal _redis client so RateLimiter can share it — a minor leaky abstraction that loosens the broker's encapsulation, though pragmatic for avoiding a second connection.

strengths: RateLimiter is a dedicated class following the existing class-per-concern pattern (RedisBroker, MessageStore, ChannelRegistry) rather than bolting logic into the server.
MessageStore.query() implements has_more pagination correctly using the limit+1 probe, returns chronological order, and the _row_to_message staticmethod refactor DRYs up row conversion.
MessageStore.expire() safely no-ops on non-positive TTL and the background cleanup task is wired at server startup.
New knobs (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS, cleanup interval) follow the established env-var config pattern, with _env_int() providing safe fallback.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped cross-cutting session (rate limiting, history queries, TTL expiry) that slots cleanly into the existing class-per-concern and env-config architecture; the measured convention score of 0.71 is dragged down solely by naming violations in the new test files, while production code adheres to the codebase's patterns.

compounding_issues: The seed Flask Todo API contributed almost nothing — Session 1 discarded it wholesale, reusing only the app.py module name as a CLI entry point, so the story was effectively greenfield from the seed

notification_server.py grew into a 357-line monolith through Sessions 1-3 before Session 4 was forced to extract transport.py; had the refactor been deferred to a later feature session, the file would have become unwieldy

Session 3's graceful-degradation design (Redis present vs. absent) created two parallel code paths, and Session 5 duplicated that pattern in the rate limiter (Redis counter + local fallback), doubling the surface that must stay correct
key_decisions: Greenfield rewrite to asyncio + websockets in Session 1, replacing the Flask seed while repurposing app.py as the server's CLI entry point
Adding the channel/subscribe-unsubscribe model in Session 2 (before any integration work), establishing the subscription topology that the routing layer later depended on
Session 3 integrated Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence with graceful degradation when Redis is unavailable, enabling multi-server fan-out and durable message history
Session 4 extracted a BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport into transport.py, decoupling connection lifecycle from message routing via on_connect/on_disconnect/on_message callbacks
Session 5 layered cross-cutting concerns cleanly on that seam: per-client per-minute rate limiting and message TTL retention with a background cleanup loop plus /history endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean, working single-file WebSocket server (broadcast/direct/system) with a passing test suite; Session 2 added channels and subscribe/unsubscribe with HTTP introspection endpoints; Session 3 integrated Redis pub/sub fan-out and SQLite persistence with tests that skip cleanly when Redis is absent; Session 4 was a structure-improving refactor that extracted the transport abstraction at 357 lines of peak monolith size; Session 5 then demonstrated the refactor paid off by stacking rate limiting and message-retention features without touching transport internals. The test suite grew from 91 to 242 lines alongside the code, and all 10 tests pass at the end.
story_review.summary: A well-ordered, coherent five-session build that progressed from a single-file WebSocket server to a tested multi-transport notification platform with channels, Redis fan-out, persistence, rate limiting, and retention — quality improved steadily and each session landed a tested, integrated capability.
